paragraphs.title: Rejection of the Partnership and Opposition to the Building

answers: The adversaries of Judah and Benjamin
The kings of Persia
The governors beyond the river
easy.explanation: The adversaries came to Zerubbabel and the chief of the fathers and offered to build with them.
easy.q: Who offered to help build the temple?

answers: Rehum and Shimshai
Zerubbabel and the chief of the fathers
Cyrus and Darius
easy.explanation: They came to Zerubbabel and to the chief of the fathers.
easy.q: To whom did the adversaries make their offer?

answers: They accepted the offer immediately
They asked them to wait
They rejected the offer
easy.explanation: They said, “Ye have nothing to do with us to build an house unto our God.”
easy.q: How did Zerubbabel, Jeshua, and the leaders respond?

answers: They would build themselves, as King Cyrus had commanded
There was no room at the building site
The king had forbidden them to speak
medium.explanation: They said that they themselves would build unto the LORD, as Cyrus had commanded them.
medium.q: Why did the leaders of Judah reject the partnership?

answers: They left the land
They weakened, troubled, and frustrated the builders
They secretly joined the builders
medium.explanation: They weakened the hands of Judah, troubled them, and hired counsellors against them.
medium.q: What did the opponents do after their offer was rejected?

answers: They encouraged the people
They taught the people to build
They discouraged and hindered the people
medium.explanation: The expression describes efforts to discourage the people and stop their work.
medium.q: What does “weakened the hands” mean in this context?

answers: The offer was not the only way they opposed the building
The builders asked for their help
The building was completed immediately
challenge.explanation: After their offer was rejected, the opponents turned to weakening and frustrating the work.
challenge.q: What can be inferred from the change from an offer of partnership to opposition?

answers: Only on the first day of building
From the days of Cyrus until the reign of Darius
Only after the reign of Darius
challenge.explanation: The opposition continued all the days of Cyrus, even until the reign of Darius.
challenge.q: During what period did this opposition continue?

answers: They were unrelated groups without leadership
They would build together according to Cyrus’s command
The building belonged only to the king of Persia
challenge.explanation: Zerubbabel said, “we ourselves together will build unto the LORD God of Israel.”
challenge.q: What does Zerubbabel’s answer emphasize about the builders?

paragraphs.title: The Accusatory Letters and the Aramaic Petition

answers: The kings of Persia
The chief of the fathers
The builders of the temple
easy.explanation: They wrote accusations against the inhabitants of Judah and Jerusalem to the Persian kings.
easy.q: To whom did the opponents send accusations?

answers: Cyrus
Artaxerxes
Darius only
easy.explanation: The passage says, “in the days of Artaxerxes.”
easy.q: During whose reign was the letter of Rehum and Shimshai written?

answers: Hebrew only
Persian only
The Syrian tongue
easy.explanation: The writing was written and interpreted in the Syrian tongue.
easy.q: In what language was the letter written and interpreted?

answers: The writers of the letter to the king
The leaders of the temple builders
The kings of Persia
medium.explanation: Rehum was the chancellor and Shimshai was the scribe who wrote against Jerusalem.

answers: Only the people of Judah
Their companions and various groups from the region
Only the temple officials
medium.explanation: The letter was sent by Rehum, Shimshai, and the rest of their companions, including several regional groups.
medium.q: Who was included with Rehum and Shimshai in the letter?

answers: A letter of praise
A list of taxes
A charge or claim of wrongdoing
medium.explanation: The letter was intended to charge the inhabitants of Judah and oppose their work.

answers: It was presented as an appeal from many regional authorities
It was written in the name of only one man
It was a private letter with no importance
challenge.explanation: The letter names many groups and officials from Samaria and beyond the river.
challenge.q: What does the listing of many groups suggest about the appeal to the king?

answers: The Syrian letter is an example of the accusations
The letter cancels all the accusations
The letter was sent by the builders of Jerusalem
challenge.explanation: The passage first mentions accusations and then gives an official letter sent to the king.
challenge.q: What is the relationship between the accusations in the opening verses and the Syrian letter?

answers: It was intended for an official administrative setting
It was written as a private work
It was meant only to be read in the temple
challenge.explanation: The language and translation fit an official petition addressed to the king and his administrators.
challenge.q: What does the use of the Syrian tongue suggest about the letter?

answers: As a peaceful city
As a rebellious and bad city
As an empty city only
easy.explanation: They called it “the rebellious and the bad city.”
easy.q: How did the writers describe Jerusalem?

answers: The city, its walls, and its foundations
A palace for the king of Persia
Only a new road
easy.explanation: They said the Jews were building the city, setting up its walls, and joining the foundations.
easy.q: What did the writers claim the Jews were building in Jerusalem?

answers: The stopping of tax payments
The loss of the record books
A shortage of builders
easy.explanation: They claimed that toll, tribute, and custom would no longer be paid.
easy.q: What harm to the king did the writers claim would result?

answers: The rebuilding would strengthen Persian rule
The rebuilding could weaken Persian control beyond the river
The rebuilding had nothing to do with government
medium.explanation: They claimed the king would have no portion beyond the river if the city were rebuilt.
medium.q: What connection did the writers make between rebuilding Jerusalem and Persian rule?

answers: To portray Jerusalem as a threat to the king’s revenue
To request freedom from taxes
To praise the people of Jerusalem
medium.explanation: They argued that rebuilding the city would cause toll, tribute, and custom to cease.
medium.q: Why did the writers mention the stopping of taxes?

answers: A tax or payment
A wall
A military command
medium.explanation: Toll is listed with tribute and custom as payments made to the king.
medium.q: What does “toll” mean in this passage?

answers: They presented it as a political and financial threat
They claimed it would benefit the royal treasury
They asked to participate in building the temple
challenge.explanation: They connected the rebuilding with rebellion, lost taxes, and weakened Persian authority.
challenge.q: How did the writers try to convince the king that rebuilding was dangerous?

answers: Rebuilding the city, stopping payments, and harming royal rule
Building the temple, celebrating, and gaining victory
Appointing officials, collecting taxes, and enlarging the army
challenge.explanation: The writers presented rebuilding the city as a cause of financial loss and political danger.
challenge.q: What is the main sequence of claims in the letter?

answers: It portrayed the danger as an ancient and continuing problem
It proved that the city had never existed
It announced that the city was loyal to the king
challenge.explanation: The claim was meant to persuade the king that Jerusalem had a long history of rebellion.
challenge.q: What rhetorical purpose did the claim that Jerusalem had been rebellious “of old time” serve?

paragraphs.title: The King’s Order to Halt Construction

answers: Rehum, Shimshai, and their companions
Zerubbabel, Jeshua, and Cyrus
Cyrus and Darius
easy.explanation: The answer was sent to Rehum, Shimshai, and the rest of their companions.
easy.q: To whom did Artaxerxes send his answer?

answers: The book of the records
The vessels of the temple
Only the names of the builders
easy.explanation: He commanded that a search be made in the book of the records of their fathers.
easy.q: What did the king command them to search?

answers: Until the end of Cyrus’s reign
Until another commandment was given
Until the builders apologized
easy.explanation: The city was not to be built until another commandment was given by the king.
easy.q: Until when did the king command the building to stop?

answers: He ordered a search of the records of the past
He immediately sent gifts to Jerusalem
He ended Persian rule beyond the river
medium.explanation: He commanded a search of the records to learn about Jerusalem’s past.
medium.q: What did the king do after reading the accusations?

answers: The city had always been loyal
The city had been connected with rebellion and harm to kings
The records contained no information
medium.explanation: The records were said to show that the city had made insurrection and sedition against kings.
medium.q: What did the search reveal according to the king’s reply?

answers: Issue an order or command
Write a blessing
Collect taxes
medium.explanation: The king was directing the officials to command the men to cease building.
medium.q: What does “Give ye now commandment” mean in the king’s order?

answers: He had Jerusalem’s past examined before issuing the order
He ordered the records to be destroyed
He relied only on the builders’ testimony
challenge.explanation: He ordered a search of the records and then acted on the reported history of rebellion.
challenge.q: How did the king use the records in making his decision?

answers: The officials were to carry out the order carefully so the kings would not be harmed
They were to continue the building secretly
They were to give Jerusalem to the builders
challenge.explanation: The king warned them to act so that no further harm would come to royal interests.
challenge.q: What does the warning not to let damage grow mean?

answers: The claims about rebellion and taxes led to the order to stop building
The claims caused the king to approve the building
The order concerned only the language of the letter
challenge.explanation: The king accepted the claim that the rebuilding threatened his rule and ordered it stopped.
challenge.q: What is the connection between the letter’s claims and the king’s order?

paragraphs.title: Execution of the Decree and the Halt of the Temple Work

answers: Rehum, Shimshai, and their companions
Zerubbabel, Jeshua, and Cyrus
Only the temple officials
easy.explanation: Rehum, Shimshai, and their companions went up in haste to Jerusalem.
easy.q: Who went up to Jerusalem after the king’s command was read?

answers: By force and power
By inviting them to a feast
By waiting for the builders’ agreement
easy.explanation: They made the Jews cease by force and power.
easy.q: How did the officials stop the Jews’ work?

answers: Until the second year of Darius’s reign
Until the first year of Cyrus’s reign
Until the end of Artaxerxes’s reign only
easy.explanation: The work ceased unto the second year of the reign of Darius king of Persia.
easy.q: Until when did the work of the house of God cease?

answers: They left their authority
They went quickly to Jerusalem and stopped the work
They built the house of God themselves
medium.explanation: They went up in haste to Jerusalem and made the Jews cease.
medium.q: What did Rehum and Shimshai do immediately after the king’s letter was read?

answers: The work of the house of God ceased
Jerusalem became independent
Taxes were immediately increased
medium.explanation: The passage says, “Then ceased the work of the house of God.”
medium.q: What was the direct result of carrying out the king’s command?

answers: Quickly and urgently
Joyfully
In complete secrecy
medium.explanation: They went to Jerusalem quickly after the king’s command was read.
medium.q: What does “in haste” mean in this passage?

answers: The command was never carried out
The command was brought to Jerusalem and enforced by force
The command was canceled before it arrived
challenge.explanation: The officials read the command, went to Jerusalem, and stopped the work by force and power.
challenge.q: How is the relationship between the royal command and the actual stopping of the work described?

answers: The stoppage lasted for a defined period and was temporary
The temple had already been completed under Cyrus
The command came only after the walls were completed
challenge.explanation: The verse identifies the point in time until which the work remained stopped.
challenge.q: What does the reference to the second year of Darius emphasize?

answers: The stoppage was forceful and compulsory
The action was merely symbolic
The builders fully agreed with it
challenge.explanation: The phrase shows that the work was stopped through coercive authority.
challenge.q: What does “by force and power” reveal about how the order was carried out?
